Current EoE treatment strategies aim to suppress esophageal inflammation and prevent long-term complications. To date, three pharmacologic agents have been approved: dupilumab ( 4 ) and two oral formulations of budesonide ( 5 , 6 ). Advances in our understanding of EoE immunopathogenesis have enabled the development of targeted biologic therapies that modulate key mediators of type 2 inflammation. These include monoclonal antibodies directed against the interleukin (IL)-4 receptor alpha (dupilumab) ( 7 , 8 ); IL-13 (cendakimab) ( 9 , 10 ); IL-5 (mepolizumab, reslizumab) ( 11 , 12 ); and the IL-5 receptor (benralizumab) ( 13 ). Additional investigational agents include lirentelimab, an anti-Siglec-8 monoclonal antibody that selectively depletes eosinophils ( 14 ), and etrasimod, an oral sphingosine-1-phosphate receptor modulator that impairs lymphocyte trafficking to inflamed tissues ( 15 ).

A prior network meta-analysis (NMA) focused largely on histologic endpoints across the available pharmacologic therapies. Most corticosteroid studies included in this review followed patients for 6–8 weeks (with a few extending to 12 weeks), whereas many biologic trials reported outcomes at 12 or 24 weeks. Because outcomes were not uniformly stratified by time point, aligning comparisons across interventions was challenging and may have contributed to variability in the findings ( 16 ).

To address these limitations, we conducted a comparative analysis of individual biologic agents, proton pump inhibitors (PPIs), and corticosteroids at 12, 24, and 48 weeks, focusing on key EoE outcomes—reduction of dysphagia and histological remission, as well as improvement in endoscopic appearance measured by the Eosinophilic Esophagitis Endoscopic Reference Score (EREFS). Our analyses are intended to inform clinical decision-making and optimize treatment strategies for patients with EoE. The certainty of evidence across all treatment comparisons was assessed using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation (GRADE) framework adapted for network meta-analysis ( 17 ).

Methods Protocol and Registration We adhered to the network version of the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, which provide a standardized framework for reporting the methodology and findings of systematic reviews and network meta-analyses ( 18 ) ( Supplementary File ). The protocol was registered in PROSPERO under CRD420261281588.

Literature Search We systematically searched the PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science databases from inception to May 25, 2025, for randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that met the predefined eligibility criteria. To ensure the search remained current prior to manuscript submission, an updated search was performed in January 2026 using the same search strategy and eligibility criteria.

In addition, we conducted manual screening of ongoing and unpublished trials on ClinicalTrials.gov and the WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). Our search strategy incorporated key terms related to “EoE,” “steroid medications,” “PPI,” “biological therapy,” and “monoclonal antibodies” ( eTable S1 ).

Eligibility Criteria and Study Selection Two reviewers independently screened the titles and abstracts, followed by full-text assessment of studies that met the inclusion criteria. Eligible studies were RCTs enrolling adolescents or adults (≥12 years) with EoE as per contemporaneous diagnostic criteria, comparing topical/systemic corticosteroids, biologic agents, or PPIs against placebo or another active intervention, with a minimum follow-up of 12 weeks. Ongoing or unpublished trials with results available through conference proceedings, ClinicalTrials.gov , or the WHO ICTRP were also included.

We excluded trials limited to pediatric patients <12 years, studies with follow-up <12 weeks, studies focused on eosinophilic gastritis, studies with overlapping data, and non-randomized studies. Data Extraction and Outcomes Two reviewers independently extracted data using a standardized Excel form with two sheets. The first captured study and baseline characteristics: author, year, country, trial phase, follow-up duration, study groups (intervention/control), sample size, gender, age, disease duration, prior glucocorticosteroid use, and dysphagia scale.

Key outcomes included changes in dysphagia from baseline and histologic remission (≤6 eosinophils/high-power field [eos/hpf]) at 12, 24, and 48 weeks. Because dysphagia instruments varied (Dysphagia Symptom Questionnaire [DSQ], Eosinophilic Esophagitis Activity Index [EEsAI], Dysphagia Symptom Diary [DSD], modified DSD), we calculated standardized mean differences (SMDs). We oriented all scales so that positive values indicated improvement.

Additional outcomes were change in endoscopic features of EoE as measured with the EREFS score at 12, 24, and 48 weeks (EREFS was analyzed as a continuous change score higher values denote worse endoscopic abnormalities; decreases reflect improvement), change in EoE-HSS grade and stage (0–3) at 24 weeks; absolute change in peak eosinophil count at 12 weeks and percentage change in peak eosinophil count at 24 weeks; and histologic response (<15 eos/hpf) at 12, 24, and 48 weeks.

When numerical data were not available in text/tables, we digitized figures using WebPlotDigitizer. If results were reported as least-squares means (LSMs) with standard errors (SEs), we treated LSMs as means and converted SEs to SDs using SD = SE × √n. Where studies reported medians and interquartile ranges, we used standard methods to approximate means and SDs ( 19 ). Assessment for Bias The risk of bias in the included studies was independently assessed by two reviewers using the Cochrane Risk of Bias Tool 2.0 (ROB 2.0) ( 20 ). Any disagreements were resolved through discussion with senior authors.

Clinically Meaningful Difference Clinically meaningful differences (CMDs) were defined prospectively to facilitate interpretation of effect estimates and judgments regarding imprecision. Because no validated CMD thresholds exist for EoE, we defined CMD thresholds based on methodological approaches used for synthesis of evidence in recent American Gastroenterological Association guidelines for other chronic autoimmune inflammatory gastrointestinal diseases (ulcerative colitis and Crohn’s disease) ( 21 , 22 ).

For dichotomous outcomes, we defined CMDs as an absolute risk difference (ARD) ≥10% for placebo-controlled trials and ≥5% for active-comparator trials. Because continuous outcomes were reported using different dysphagia instruments, results were standardized as SMDs and interpreted using Cohen’s criteria (0.2, 0.5, and 0.8 indicating small, moderate, and large effects) ( 23 – 25 ). We defined a clinically meaningful difference as an SMD ≥0.30 in placebo-controlled trials and ≥0.20 in active-comparator trials.

Sensitivity analyses evaluated more conservative thresholds (15% and 10% for dichotomous outcomes and SMD ≥0.50 and ≥0.40 for continuous outcomes in placebo-controlled and active-comparator settings, respectively). GRADE assessment Evidence certainty was assessed using the GRADE framework ( 17 ). Indirect estimates began at the lower certainty of the two direct comparisons forming the initial network loop, with further downgrading for imprecision or intransitivity indicating clinical or methodological heterogeneity. Network consistency, when feasible, was evaluated using node-splitting analyses comparing direct and indirect estimates.

Imprecision was assessed using CMD thresholds. Downgrading was one level if the 95% CI crossed the CMD but not the null; two if it crossed both the null and CMD in one direction; and three if it spanned benefit, no effect, and harm. If no downgrading occurred, the optimal information size (OIS) was evaluated; further downgrading was performed if the upper-to-lower CI ratio exceeded 3. Per GRADE, moderate- and low-certainty evidence were described as “likely” and “possibly” ( 26 ).

Statistical Analysis A frequentist random-effects network meta-analysis was conducted in R (version 4.2.2) using the netmeta package, following the intention-to-treat principle. Treatment effects were estimated on the log risk ratio (log-RR) scale for dichotomous outcomes. For each treatment serving as the reference in league tables, baseline risk was estimated as the pooled event rate among participants receiving that treatment across all relevant trial arms ( 27 ). ARDs were derived by applying pooled risk ratios to baseline risks using the formula: ARD = BR × (RR – 1) ( 28 ).

For continuous outcomes, SMDs with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were reported. The transitivity assumption was evaluated by comparing key clinical and methodological characteristics across treatment comparisons, including age, sex distribution, disease duration, baseline EREFS, prior glucocorticosteroid use, and baseline peak eosinophil count. Network geometry was examined to identify closed loops and assess the feasibility of formal inconsistency testing. Because most trials compared active treatments with placebo and few head-to-head comparisons between active agents were available, the network was largely star-shaped. Closed loops occurred primarily among different dosing regimens of the same agent, limiting formal inconsistency testing between distinct active treatments. Statistical heterogeneity was assessed using the I 2 statistic, with values >50% indicating substantial heterogeneity ( 29 ). Publication bias was evaluated by visual inspection of funnel plots and formally tested using Egger’s regression test.

Intervention rankings were derived using the Surface Under the Cumulative Ranking (SUCRA) curve, with higher values indicating more favorable outcomes. However, SUCRA values should be interpreted alongside the magnitude of effect estimates and their associated uncertainty, rather than in isolation ( 30 ). Conclusions regarding comparative efficacy were based primarily on the effect estimates and their certainty of evidence, with SUCRA rankings presented as supplementary information rather than as the basis for inference.

An arm-based mixed-effects meta-regression was implemented with the metafor package to evaluate the impact of baseline patient characteristics on treatment effects ( 31 ). Within-study dependence among multiple effect sizes was addressed by applying this method ( 32 , 33 ). Covariate selection was guided by clinical relevance and by consistency in reporting across studies. Sex and age were entered as covariates in the model. Result: Studies Characteristics A total of 7,393 records were identified through database searches, of which 12 studies comprising 13 RCTs were included ( 7 – 10 , 12 – 15 , 34 – 37 ), as one study included two separate trials ( Figure 1 ).

Of the 13 included RCTs, 11 were published as full-text articles ( 7 – 9 , 12 , 13 , 15 , 34 – 37 ), while two were completed but unpublished at the time of analysis; however, their final results were available on ClinicalTrials.gov ( NCT04322708 , NCT04753697 ) ( 10 , 14 ). Six trials were Phase III studies ( 7 , 10 , 13 , 34 , 37 ), one was a combined Phase II/III trial ( 14 ), and the remaining six were Phase II trials ( 8 , 9 , 12 , 15 , 35 , 36 ). Among the 13 RCTs included, 11 evaluated induction of remission at 12 or 24 weeks in active EoE ( 7 – 9 , 12 – 15 , 34 – 36 ); one evaluated induction at 24 weeks followed by maintenance at 48 weeks ( 10 ); and one evaluated maintenance of remission alone at 48 weeks ( 37 ).

Overall, the 13 trials enrolled a total of 2,163 participants. The distribution of interventions was as follows: dupilumab 300mg (n = 145), benralizumab 30mg (n = 103), mepolizumab 300mg (n = 32), cendakimab 360mg (n = 320), lirentelimab 1mg/kg (n = 93), lirentelimab 3mg/kg (n = 91), etrasimod 2mg (n = 41), etrasimod 1mg (n = 39), budesonide oral suspension (BOS) 2mg (n = 264), APT-1011 3mg twice daily (BID) (n = 20), APT-1011 3mg horasomni (at bedtime; HS) (n = 21), APT-1011 1.5mg BID (n = 22), APT-1011 1.5 mgHS (n = 21), budesonide orodispersible tablets (BOT) 0.5mg (n=68), BOT 1mg (n=68), and placebo (n = 813) ( eTable S2 ).

Risk of Bias and Publication Bias Two trials were judged at low risk of bias, while eleven raised some concerns ( eFigure S1 ). Egger’s test showed no evidence of publication bias for dysphagia (P=0.25 at 12 weeks; P=0.40 at 24 weeks) or histologic remission (P=0.99 at 12 weeks; P=0.74 at 24 weeks) ( eFigure S2 ).

Improvement in the Dysphagia symptom At 12 weeks, the NMA included 1,676 patients across eight interventions, including placebo ( Figure 2A ). Dupilumab 300mg was associated with a high-certainty improvement in dysphagia compared with placebo, whereas cendakimab 360mg and BOS 2mg demonstrated moderate-certainty benefit, with SMDs ranging from −0.31 to −0.54 ( eTable S3 ). Dupilumab 300mg also showed moderate-to-high-certainty benefit compared with lirentelimab at both 1mg/kg and 3mg/kg, as well as compared with benralizumab 30mg, with SMDs of −0.69, −0.42, and −0.65, respectively. In contrast, cendakimab 360mg and BOS 2mg demonstrated moderate-certainty benefit only when compared with lirentelimab 1mg/kg and benralizumab 30mg, with SMDs ranging from −0.31 to −0.50. The sensitivity analysis indicated that Dupilumab 300mg shifted from high-to moderate-certainty benefit relative to placebo, lirentelimab 1 mg/kg, and benralizumab 30mg ( eTable S4 ).

Direct pairwise comparisons confirmed the superiority of dupilumab 300mg, cendakimab 360mg, and BOS 2mg over placebo ( eFigure S2 ). Based on SUCRA, dupilumab 300mg ranked highest in symptomatic efficacy (92%) ( eFigure S6A ). No heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 0%). At 24 weeks, the NMA included 1,194 patients across eight interventions ( Figure 2B ). Dupilumab 300mg demonstrated a sustained high-certainty benefit, while cendakimab 360mg showed a sustained moderate-certainty benefit compared with placebo, with SMDs of −0.64 and −0.34, respectively ( eTable S5 ).

Dupilumab 300mg also showed high-to moderate-certainty benefit compared with lirentelimab at both 1mg/kg and 3mg/kg, etrasimod 1mg, and benralizumab 30mg, with SMDs of −0.79, −0.42, −0.56, and −0.78, respectively. In contrast, cendakimab 360mg demonstrated moderate-certainty benefit only when compared with lirentelimab 1 mg/kg and benralizumab 30mg, with SMDs of −0.49 and −0.50, respectively. Sensitivity analyses indicated that the certainty of benefit for dupilumab 300mg relative to placebo was downgraded from high to moderate ( eTable S6 ).

Direct comparisons confirmed the supcriority of dupilumab 300mg and cendakimab 360mg over placebo ( eFigure S4 ). SUCRA again ranked dupilumab 300mg as the most effective treatment (97%) ( eFigure S6B ). No heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 0%).

At 48 weeks, the NMA included 470 patients across five interventions ( Figure 2C ). BOT 0.5mg and BOT 1mg were associated with high-certainty improvement in dysphagia compared with placebo, with SMDs of −1.19 and −1.43, respectively. Both doses also demonstrated high-certainty benefit compared with cendakimab 360mg administered weekly or every two weeks, with SMDs ranging from −0.89 to −1.17 ( eTable S7 ). Sensitivity analyses yielded similar findings ( eTable S8 ).

Direct comparisons confirmed the superiority of BOT 0.5mg and 1mg over placebo, while no differences were observed between cendakimab 360mg weekly and every two weeks compared with placebo ( eFigure S5 ). According to SUCRA, BOT 1mg ranked as the most effective treatment (96%) ( eFigure S6C ). Heterogeneity could not be assessed.

Histological remission At 12 weeks, the NMA included 619 patients across eight interventions ( Figure 2D ). All interventions demonstrated moderate-certainty benefit compared with placebo, with RRs ranging from 9.05 to 28.76 ( eTable S9 ). Sensitivity analyses yielded similar findings ( eTable S10 ). Direct comparisons confirmed the superiority of each intervention over placebo ( eFigure S7 ). SUCRA identified BOS 2mg as the most effective intervention (78%) ( eFigure S10A ). No heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 0%).

At 24 weeks, the NMA included 1,212 patients across eight interventions ( Figure 2E ). All interventions except etrasimod (1mg and 2mg) demonstrated moderate-certainty benefit compared with placebo, with RRs ranging from 8.09 to 13.36 ( eTable S11 ). Sensitivity analyses yielded consistent results ( eTable S12 ). Direct comparisons yielded results similar to those of the indirect comparisons ( eFigure S8 ). SUCRA ranked benralizumab 30mg as the most effective intervention (80%) ( eFigure S10B ). No heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 0%).

At 48 weeks, the NMA included 498 patients across five interventions ( Figure 2F ). All interventions demonstrated moderate-certainty benefit compared with placebo, with RRs ranging from 5.86 to 8.71 ( eTable S13 ). Sensitivity analyses yielded similar findings ( eTable S14 ). Direct comparison results were consistent with the network estimates ( eFigure S9 ). According to SUCRA analysis, BOT 1mg ranked as the most effective treatment (79%) ( eFigure S10C ). Heterogeneity could not be assessed.

Improvement in EREFS At 12 weeks, the NMA included 619 patients across eight interventions ( eFigure S11 ). Dupilumab 300mg and APT-1011 (3mg HS and 1.5 mg BID) yielded high-certainty evidence of benefit, whereas BOS 2mg and APT-1011 (1.5mg HS and 3 mg BID) provided moderate-certainty evidence of benefit relative to placebo, with SMDs between −0.56 and −1.33 ( eTable S15 ). Sensitivity analyses reduced the certainty rating for the benefit of dupilumab 300mg and APT-1011 1.5 mg BID versus placebo from high to moderate ( eTable S16 ). These findings were corroborated by direct pairwise comparisons ( eFigure S12 ). According to SUCRA, APT-1011 3mg HS ranked highest (86%) ( eFigure S15A ). Substantial heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 53.3%).

At 24 weeks, the NMA included 1,170 patients across eight interventions ( eFigure S11 ). Dupilumab 300mg and cendakimab 360mg demonstrated high-certainty evidence of benefit, whereas etrasimod 2mg showed moderate-certainty benefit relative to placebo (SMDs: −1.16, −1.01, and −0.49, respectively) ( eTable S17 ). Dupilumab also demonstrated moderate-to-high certainty benefit over lirentelimab (1mg/kg and 3mg/kg), etrasimod (1mg and 2mg), and benralizumab 30mg (SMDs: −1.21, −1.29, −0.83, −0.66, and −1.10, respectively). Cendakimab 360mg showed moderate-to-high certainty benefit over etrasimod 1mg, lirentelimab (1mg/kg and 3mg/kg), and benralizumab 30 mg (SMDs: −0.68, −1.07, −1.15, and −0.96, respectively). In sensitivity analyses, the certainty of benefit for dupilumab 300mg compared with etrasimod 1mg was downgraded from high to moderate ( eTable S18 ). Direct comparisons with placebo supported these results ( eFigure S13 ). Dupilumab 300mg was ranked as the most effective treatment by SUCRA (96%) ( eFigure S15B ). No heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 0%).

At 48 weeks, the NMA included 482 patients across five interventions ( eFigure S11 ). All active treatments demonstrated high-certainty evidence of benefit compared with placebo, with SMDs ranging from −0.76 to −1.96 ( eTable S19 ). BOT 0.5mg and 1mg also demonstrated high-certainty benefit compared with cendakimab 360mg administered either weekly or every two weeks, with SMDs ranging from −1.18 to – 1.20. Sensitivity analyses reduced the certainty rating for the benefit of cendakimab 360mg once weekly and once every two weeks versus placebo from high to moderate ( eTable S20 ).

Direct comparisons against placebo were consistent with the indirect analysis ( eFigure S14 ). Based on SUCRA rankings, BOT 0.5mg and 1mg were identified as the most effective interventions (88%) ( eFigure S15C ). Heterogeneity could not be assessed.

Improvement in EOE-HSS grade score. At 24 weeks, the NMA included 708 patients across five interventions ( eFigure S16A ). Dupilumab 300mg, cendakimab 360mg, and etrasimod (1mg and 2mg) demonstrated high-certainty benefit over placebo, with SMDs ranging from −1.04 to −1.78 ( eTable S21 ). Dupilumab 300mg also demonstrated moderate-certainty benefit over etrasimod (1mg and 2mg) (SMDs: −0.74 and −0.63, respectively). Sensitivity analyses yielded similar findings ( eTable S22 ). Direct comparisons with placebo showed similar results ( eFigure S17A ). SUCRA ranked dupilumab 300mg highest in efficacy (97%) ( eFigure S18A ). No heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 0%).

Improvement in the EOE-HSS stage score At 24 weeks, the NMA again included 708 patients across five interventions ( eFigure S16B ). Dupilumab 300mg, cendakimab 360mg, and etrasimod (1mg and 2mg) demonstrated high-certainty improvement relative to placebo, with SMDs ranging from −1.08 to −1.89 ( eTable S23 ). Dupilumab 300mg also demonstrated moderate-to-high certainty benefit over cendakimab 360mg and etrasimod (1mg and 2mg) (SMDs: −0.47, −0.81, and −0.65, respectively). In sensitivity analyses, the certainty of benefit for dupilumab 300mg compared with etrasimod 1mg was downgraded from high to moderate ( eTable S24 ). Direct pairwise comparisons with placebo supported these findings ( eFigure S17B ). SUCRA ranked dupilumab 300mg as the most effective treatment (99%) ( eFigure S18B ). No heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 0%).

Change in peak eosinophilic count At 12 weeks, the NMA included 516 patients across four interventions and assessed absolute change in peak eosinophil count ( eFigure S19A ). Dupilumab 300mg, mepolizumab 300mg, and BOS 2mg demonstrated high-certainty benefits compared with placebo, with SMDs ranging from −0.99 to −2.33 ( eTable S25 ). Dupilumab 300mg also demonstrated a high-certainty benefit over mepolizumab 300mg and BOS 2mg (SMDs: −1.19 and −1.24, respectively). In sensitivity analyses, the certainty of benefit for dupilumab 300mg compared with mepolizumab 300mg was downgraded from high to moderate ( eTable S26 ). The superiority over placebo was confirmed in direct comparisons ( eFigure S20A ). SUCRA ranked dupilumab 300mg highest (100%) ( eFigure S21A ). No heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 0%).

At 24 weeks, the NMA included 450 patients across three interventions and assessed percentage change in peak eosinophil count ( eFigure S19B ). Benralizumab 30mg and dupilumab 300mg demonstrated high-certainty benefit compared with placebo (SMDs: −1.44 and −1.23, respectively) ( eTable S27 ). Sensitivity analyses yielded similar findings ( eTable S28 ). The superiority of these interventions over placebo was confirmed by direct comparisons ( eFigure S20B ). Benralizumab 30mg ranked highest in SUCRA (87%) ( eFigure S21B ). Moderate heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 43.3%).

Histological response At 12 weeks, the NMA included 532 patients across eight interventions ( eFigure S22A ). All interventions demonstrated moderate-certainty benefit over placebo, with RRs ranging from 12.67 to 65.07 ( eTable S29 ). Sensitivity analyses yielded similar findings ( eTable S30 ). Direct comparisons confirmed the superiority of each intervention over placebo ( eFigure S23 ). SUCRA identified BOS 2mg as the most effective intervention (89%) ( eFigure S26A ). Heterogeneity could not be assessed.

At 24 weeks, the NMA included 1,212 patients across eight interventions ( eFigure S22B ). All interventions demonstrated moderate-certainty benefit compared with placebo, with RRs ranging from 5.78 to 11.40 ( eTable S31 ). Sensitivity analyses yielded comparable results ( eTable S32 ). Direct comparisons with placebo confirmed these findings ( eFigure S24 ). Cendakimab 360mg was ranked as the most effective intervention (76%) by SUCRA ( eFigure S26B ). No heterogeneity was observed (I 2 = 0%).

At 48 weeks, the NMA included 498 patients across five interventions ( eFigure S22C ). All treatments showed moderate-certainty benefit over placebo, with RRs ranging from 5.86 to 8.71 ( eTable S33 ). Sensitivity analyses supported the primary findings ( eTable S34 ). Direct comparisons confirmed the superiority of each intervention over placebo ( eFigure S25 ). According to SUCRA, BOT 1mg ranked as the most effective intervention (79%) ( eFigure S26C ). Heterogeneity could not be assessed.

Meta-regression Age and sex were reported in all included studies and were therefore incorporated into the meta-regression analyses. Other potentially relevant variables, including PPI use, corticosteroid treatment, and baseline eosinophil count, were not consistently reported across trials and could not be included in the models. Meta-regression analyses did not identify significant effect modification by male proportion or increasing age for changes in dysphagia symptoms at 12 and 24 weeks, EREFS at 24 weeks, or peak eosinophil count at 12 and 24 weeks. However, increasing age was associated with a greater change in EREFS at 12 weeks ( eTable S35 ).

DISCUSSION In this NMA, we evaluated the comparative efficacy of biologic and swallowed topical steroid therapies in EoE, focusing on clinical, histologic, and endoscopic outcomes at 12, 24, and 48 weeks. Results were available only for BOS, mepolizumab, and APT-1011 at 12 weeks, while data for etrasimod and lirentelimab were available only at 24 weeks. Data were available for dupilumab and benralizumab at both 12 and 24 weeks. Data for cendakimab were available at 12, 24, and 48 weeks, whereas results for BOT were available only at 48 weeks. No RCTs meeting our inclusion criteria for PPIs were identified. The primary outcomes in our NMA, patient symptoms (reduction in dysphagia) and histologic remission, were chosen to be in line with the US Food and Drug Administration guidance on EoE trials. The certainty of evidence for all comparisons was evaluated using the GRADE tool.

In terms of dysphagia reduction, dupilumab 300mg, cendakimab 360mg, and BOS 2mg demonstrated moderate-to-high-certainty benefits over placebo. These agents also showed moderate-to-high-certainty benefit and outperformed several active comparators, including benralizumab 30mg and lirentelimab 1mg/kg, with dupilumab 300mg additionally surpassing lirentelimab 3mg/kg and etrasimod 1mg. Conversely, BOT 0.5mg and 1mg showed high-certainty benefit over both cendakimab 360mg and placebo at 48 weeks.

For histologic remission, all agents showed moderate certainty benefit over placebo except etrasimod. All agents, including etrasimod, also demonstrated moderate certainty benefit compared with placebo for the secondary outcome of histologic response. Other secondary histologic outcomes were also examined. Dupilumab 300mg, cendakimab 360mg, and etrasimod (1mg and 2mg) were all superior, with moderate certainty, to placebo for both EoE-HS grade and stage scores. Notably, dupilumab 300mg showed moderate certainty benefit and outperformed etrasimod across both doses for grade scores and was superior to both cendakimab and etrasimod across both doses for stage scores.

Reductions in peak eosinophil counts compared to placebo were achieved with dupilumab 300mg, mepolizumab 300mg, BOS 2mg, and benralizumab 30mg, with dupilumab demonstrating greater reductions than both mepolizumab and BOS. All were supported by high certainty evidence. Assessment of endoscopic improvement, as measured by the EREFS, showed that ATP-1011 (all doses), BOS 2mg, dupilumab 300mg, cendakimab 360mg, and etrasimod 2mg had moderate certainty of benefit and were more effective than placebo. Additionally, dupilumab 300mg and cendakimab 360mg showed moderate-to-high-certainty benefits compared with etrasimod 1mg, benralizumab 30mg, and lirentelimab 1mg/kg. Dupilumab 300mg also showed superiority over etrasimod 2 mg.

Taken together, the symptom and endoscopic outcomes highlight dupilumab 300mg, cendakimab 360mg, and BOS 2mg as valuable therapeutic options with moderate certainty of benefit for the management of EoE within a 12-week timeframe. All three were also effective in achieving histologic remission and response, while dupilumab 300mg showed superior results in other secondary histologic outcomes, including EoE-HSS and changes in peak eosinophil count. While dupilumab and cendakimab demonstrated sustained efficacy through 24 weeks, the long-term effectiveness of BOS 2mg remains to be established, as all trials with BOS 2mg in our NMA were 12 weeks in duration. On the other hand, BOT (0.5 and Img) showed a high-certainty benefit over cendakimab 360mg and placebo for symptom and endoscopic outcomes at 48 weeks, but only a moderate-certainty benefit over placebo for histologic remission and response at 48 weeks. Of note, short-term BOT treatment was excluded from the comparisons, as its efficacy was assessed following only 6 weeks of induction therapy ( 38 ).

Dupilumab remains the sole biologic therapy approved by the US FDA and the European Medicines Agency (EMA) for the treatment of EoE ( 4 , 39 ), alongside two oral budesonide formulations ( 5 , 6 ). The 2025 American College of Gastroenterology (ACG) guidelines provide a conditional recommendation for dupilumab in patients aged 12 years and older who remain symptomatic despite PPI therapy, supported by moderate-quality evidence ( 40 ). However, due to limited evidence, the guidelines do not extend their recommendations to other emerging biologic agents currently under investigation.

It is now well established that symptom severity in EoE, particularly dysphagia, does not always correlate with histologic or endoscopic disease activity ( 41 , 42 ). Several explanations have been proposed for this discordance, including the presence of fixed fibrostenotic changes, which may limit symptomatic improvement even when mucosal inflammation is reduced ( 43 ), adaptive eating behaviors that may mask dysphagia ( 44 ), or concomitant oesophageal motility disorders ( 45 , 46 ). Prior esophageal dilation may also influence clinical outcomes independently of histologic response ( 47 , 48 ). Among patients treated with BOS, histologic responses were similar regardless of dilation history; however, those with prior dilation were less likely to achieve symptomatic improvement, while modestly greater improvements in EREFS were observed ( 47 ). These findings suggest that dilation history may reflect underlying fibrostenotic disease and may confound the relationship between symptomatic improvement and anti-inflammatory therapy. However, in the NMA, baseline disease characteristics were well balanced between intervention and placebo groups, making it less likely that differences in initial disease severity account for the observed dissociation between clinical and histologic outcomes.

Another consideration is the limited clinical impact of targeting the IL-5 and Siglec-8 pathways in isolation. While IL-5-directed therapies such as benralizumab and mepolizumab, and Siglec-8-directed therapy such as lirentelimab, effectively reduce tissue eosinophil counts, they have not consistently demonstrated symptomatic benefit in either direct or indirect comparisons. These findings suggest that although eosinophils play a central role in the pathogenesis and diagnosis of EoE ( 49 , 50 ), they may not be the sole drivers of disease activity. As a T cell-mediated disorder, EoE involves multiple immune pathways and inflammatory mediators beyond eosinophils ( 50 ).

In comparison to agents targeting a single pathway, such as the IL-5 pathway, topical corticosteroids, such as BOS and BOT, exert broader anti-inflammatory effects, targeting multiple cytokine pathways and immune cells. This broader mechanism likely contributes to their observed efficacy across histologic and symptomatic endpoints ( 37 , 38 ), making them first-line therapies for EoE and establishing them as the gold standard for new pharmacological developments. Their use has been associated with an increased risk of adverse effects, including esophageal candidiasis and potential adrenal suppression ( 51 ); however, a recent NMA has shown these risks to be no higher than those observed with placebo or PPls ( 52 ), and adherence may be impacted by the need for twice-daily administration ( 53 ).

Differences in follow-up duration limited direct comparisons of safety outcomes across studies. However, among the included trials that reported safety data, the incidence of adverse events and serious adverse events was comparable between biologic agents and placebo, and between steroid agents and placebo ( 7 , 10 , 12 – 15 ). This study has some limitations. Six of the included trials were phase II studies, particularly those comparing mepolizumab 300 mg and ATP-1011 (1.5mg and 3mg), and etrasimod (Tmg and 2mg), with sample sizes ranging from 19 to 41 participants.

Additionally, trials of PPI agents, which are the most commonly prescribed first-line treatment option for EoE ( 54 ), and most swallowed topical corticosteroids (budesonide [aerosolized/swallowed], fluticasone [aerosolized/swallowed], and BOT) had follow-up durations of only 6 to 8 weeks. To reduce heterogeneity, these trials were excluded from the analysis, as no data were available for biologic therapies with follow-up periods of less than 12 weeks. However, this exclusion represents a limitation, particularly given that therapies such as PPIs and swallowed topical corticosteroids are widely used in clinical practice, and excluding these trials may reduce the applicability of our findings.

The limited duration of most corticosteroid trials constrains our ability to assess their utility in the treatment hierarchy of EoE, especially over the long term. We identified three placebo-controlled trials of topical corticosteroids with a 12-week duration for inclusion in our analyses, but only one trial had longer follow-up. Furthermore, as mentioned above, most trials of topical corticosteroids are only 6–8 weeks in duration and therefore not useful for assessing outcomes beyond very short-term effects.

Furthermore, the scarcity of long-term data on biological therapies limits our ability to assess their utility for long-term treatment of EoE. Direct comparisons of biologic agents beyond 24 weeks were not feasible, except for cendakimab.

Our results at 48 weeks, in particular, should be interpreted with caution. First, some trials transitioned patients from placebo to the active comparator arm at 24 weeks (e.g., dupilumab, benralizumab), which prevents assessment of long-term comparative efficacy beyond 24 weeks. Second, only two trials with outcomes at 48 weeks were identified in our review: one with two doses of BOT and placebo and one with two dosing schedules of cendakimab and placebo. Furthermore, BOT was evaluated as maintenance therapy in patients already in histologic remission, whereas cendakimab was assessed in patients with active EoE undergoing induction followed by maintenance. Thus, limited data and differences in trial design necessitate caution when interpreting our findings for outcomes at 48 weeks.

Furthermore, safety data were insufficiently reported across trials, particularly regarding the comparative safety profiles of biologic and corticosteroid therapies, which remain a significant knowledge gap.

In conclusion, this analysis suggests that dupilumab 300mg, cendakimab 360mg, BOS 2mg, and BOT 0.5 mg and Img are among the most effective agents for improving both dysphagia and endoscopic outcomes in patients with EoE. All evaluated therapies—including biologies and topical corticosteroids—were effective in achieving histologic remission or response. Nonetheless, direct comparative data between biologies and corticosteroids remain limited, particularly regarding long-term efficacy, symptom resolution, and safety. Future head-to-head trials are warranted to evaluate these agents more comprehensively, with a focus on dysphagia-related outcomes, endoscopic improvement, and adverse event profiles to better guide therapeutic decision-making in EoE.

What You Need to Know BACKGROUND Biologic agents and swallowed topical steroids are increasingly used for eosinophilic esophagitis, but comparative, time-specific effects on symptoms, histology, and endoscopy in adolescents and adults remain unclear. FINDINGS Across 13 randomized trials, dupilumab, cendakimab, and oral budesonide provided consistent dysphagia improvement, while most therapies achieved histologic remission, revealing a frequent dissociation between symptom and tissue responses.

IMPLICATIONS FOR PATIENT CARE Clinicians should prioritize therapies with proven symptomatic benefit, recognize that histologic remission may not predict symptom relief, and tailor EoE treatment choices by outcome domain and treatment duration.

Abstract Background Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic, progressive, immune-mediated disease characterized by symptoms of esophageal dysfunction and a dense eosinophilic infiltration of the esophageal mucosa (≥15 eosinophils/high-power field or ≥60 eosinophils/mm 2 ). The diagnosis requires the exclusion of other local or systemic causes of esophageal eosinophilia. EoE is frequently associated with atopic disorders, including asthma, allergic rhinitis, and atopic dermatitis, reflecting its complex immunopathogenesis.

Summary Adults with active EoE may present with a broad spectrum of symptoms, most commonly dysphagia and food impaction, the latter often requiring urgent endoscopic intervention. Endoscopy plays a central role in both the diagnosis and monitoring of EoE. Although endoscopic appearances may vary, characteristic findings include edema, esophageal rings, whitish exudates, linear furrows, and strictures. These features are systematically assessed using the Endoscopic Reference Score (EREFS), which provides a standardized measure of endoscopic disease activity and severity. Recognition of these clinical manifestations and endoscopic abnormalities is essential for accurate diagnosis, disease assessment, and therapeutic management.

Key Messages EoE is a chronic inflammatory esophageal disorder with distinct clinical and endoscopic manifestations. Dysphagia and food impaction are the hallmark symptoms in adults, while endoscopic evaluation remains indispensable for diagnosis and follow-up. The use of standardized scoring systems such as EREFS improves the assessment of disease activity and facilitates consistent monitoring. Early recognition of clinical symptoms and characteristic endoscopic findings is critical for optimizing patient care and preventing long-term complications.

Over two decades ago, EoE was identified as a distinct clinicopathological syndrome [ 3 , 4 ]. Nowadays, EoE is the leading cause of chronic or recurrent dysphagia among children, adolescents, and adults in the developed world, with its incidence and prevalence on the rise [ 5 ]. EoE is three times more prevalent in males and has been mainly described in white ethnic origin patients [ 5 ]. Furthermore, EoE is linked to atopic diseases such as allergic rhinoconjunctivitis, allergic asthma, and atopic dermatitis [ 6 ]. Although there are diagnostic and therapeutic guidelines for EoE in many countries, recent studies still reveal a significant delay in the initial diagnosis of EoE [ 7 , 8 ]. The delayed diagnosis can lead to the remodeling of the esophagus due to persistent inflammatory activity, with the endoscopic counterpart being the stricture or narrowing of the esophagus [ 8 ]. There are reasons for the significantly delayed diagnosis of EoE. First, insufficient awareness and understanding of EoE and its various aspects among general practitioners and gastroenterologists result in a lack of biopsy sampling during index endoscopy. Second, EoE patients have become accustomed to their swallowing disorders and adjust their eating habits accordingly. As a result, the clinical presentation can be compensated for and concealed by patients for years. They have grown accustomed to their swallowing problems and do not deem it necessary to communicate these issues to their doctor. Third, the lack of knowledge of endoscopic EoE features and sometimes the absence of typical endoscopic signs of active EoE. This article delves into the clinical presentation of EoE patients, and furthermore, it outlines the endoscopic aspects of this chronic inflammatory condition of the esophagus.

Clinical Presentation: Symptoms in Adults Adult and adolescent patients with active EoE typically report dysphagia for solid foods, particularly foods with fibrous and very firm consistency (such as chicken, beef, apples, carrots, tablets). Since some patients have been experiencing their swallowing difficulties for years, they often struggle to accurately describe them and tend to refer to it as retrosternal discomfort. In a prospective study of 400 patients undergoing esophagogastroduodenoscopy (EGD) for esophageal symptoms, 7.3% had histological evidence of EoE. In this study, EoE was observed significantly more frequently in men, patients under 50 years of age, patients with allergic asthma, and patients with dysphagia and food impaction [ 9 ]. Another prospective study including 100 adult patients with nonobstructive dysphagia reported that 22% had EoE [ 10 ]. Food or foreign bolus obstruction (FBO) represents another frequently occurring clinical manifestation of EoE. In a retrospective study involving 546 patients with foreign bolus obstruction and available histology, 46% exhibited histological features suggestive for EoE. Furthermore, EoE was also the strongest predictor of multiple presentations with food bolus obstruction (FBO) (OR 3.5 [95% CI 1.8–7.0]) [ 11 ]. Less commonly reported symptoms in EoE include heartburn, regurgitations, and retrosternal non-swallowing-related pain (shown in Table 1 ). In a retrospective study involving over 300 patients with reflux-like symptoms, EoE was diagnosed in 7.7% when biopsies were taken during EGD [ 12 ]. In another retrospective study, 161 consecutive patients with chest pain were examined and biopsied endoscopically. Histological signs consistent with EoE were found in 6% of cases [ 13 ]. Most studies that have examined symptoms in EoE patients originate from the early 2000s and mostly have a retrospective design. Furthermore, these studies did not use a standardized biopsy protocol, often resulting in the absence of stepwise biopsies of the esophagus. These circumstances could have led to an overinterpretation of the occurrence of EoE in cases of reflux symptoms and especially erosive reflux disease. EoE and gastroesophageal reflux disease can coexist, but in my personal experience, dysphagic symptoms take precedence in EoE patients with additional observed reflux lesions during EGD. During clinical evaluation, it is important to note, especially in adolescents and adults, that patients often develop adaptive strategies and alter their eating behaviors to avoid symptoms, which can also lead to a delay in diagnosis. A study demonstrated that patients with active EoE, when consuming a standard meal compared to healthy controls, significantly chew more frequently, consume significantly more liquids, and require significantly more time for complete consumption. Therefore, during clinical evaluation, specific questions regarding eating behaviors or avoidance strategies should also be asked to better assess the clinical disease activity [ 14 ] (shown in Table 2 ). Another symptom complex recently described is the Food-induced Immediate Response of the Esophagus (FIRE). It describes an uncomfortable or painful sensation, independent of dysphagia, that occurs immediately after the contact of specific foods with the esophageal lining. In a large survey involving 57 EoE experts and 368 EoE patients, 90% of the experts and 40% of the patients reported having observed the FIRE symptom complex. The most common triggers for FIRE symptoms were fresh fruits, vegetables, and wine. In male patients with FIRE symptoms, endoscopic bolus removals were more frequent [ 15 ]. The clinical presentation of active EoE appears heterogeneous and can be obscured over years due to patients unconsciously altering their eating habits. Due to this, in patients with esophageal symptoms, an extensive and comprehensive medical history is recommended, followed by an EGD with the collection of stepwise biopsies from the esophagus [ 2 , 16 ].

Clinical Presentation: Endoscopy in Adult Patients with EoE Active EoE is often accompanied by visually evident structural changes in the esophagus during EGD. While whitish exudates/plaques (correlating with eosinophilic microabscesses on histological examination), longitudinal furrows, and mucosal edema signify acute inflammation, features like a fixed ring formation (known as “trachealization” of the esophagus), a narrow-caliber esophagus, and strictures reflect a chronic fibrotic stage [ 18 , 19 ]. Frequently observed during endoscopic passage are significant fragility of the esophageal lining (“crepe-paper sign”) and resistance during biopsy collection (“tug sign”) [ 20 , 21 ]. In adults, the most common findings include longitudinal furrows (80%), rings (64%), a narrow-caliber esophagus (28%), whitish exudates (16%), and strictures (12%) [ 22 ]. The endoscopic findings can be present individually; however, they more commonly appear in combination. While they are not necessarily present in every EoE patient, they can be detected in 90% of EoE patients. The detection rate of significant findings increases with the level of training of the endoscopist for EoE [ 23 ].

Like in other esophageal diseases where classification systems are used, such as the Los Angeles Classification for Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease and the Prague Classification for Barrett’s Esophagus, in EoE, the EREFS scoring system should be used to describe the endoscopic findings ( Fig. 1 ). The EREFS classification system (an acronym for Exudates, Rings, Edema, Furrows, and Strictures) was published by Hirano et al. [ 24 ] in 2013 and was developed to better quantitatively describe the major endoscopic findings in EoE (shown in Table 3 ). Using this system provides greater uniformity in the description of findings, identifies and discriminates between non-EoE and EoE patients, and correlates with treatment [ 25 ]. Furthermore, using the EREFS Score allows for better comparison of endoscopic findings. Another advantage of using the EREFS Score is that “we all speak the same language”. In a prospective multicenter study involving adult EoE patients, this classification showed good intra- and interobserver agreement among experts and inexperienced examiners. Other independent studies have confirmed the validity of the EREFS classification in both children and adults [ 25 – 28 ].

Rather rarely, the esophagus can appear normal on endoscopy (∼10%) in patients with active EoE. In such cases, however, step biopsies from the esophagus should still be taken. Independent predictors for a “normal-appearing esophagus” during EGD in a retrospective study were: younger age, abdominal pain, and the absence of dysphagia symptoms. After the publication of the EREFS scoring system for EoE, the frequency of an endoscopically normal esophagus decreased (∼7%) [ 29 ].

To perform an accurate EREFS classification, several things have to be considered during the EGD: initiate the assessment of the esophagus during the insertion of the endoscope and not during the withdrawal of the examination or after an endoscopic intervention such as dilation. After ruling out any obstructive factors, food residues, or fluid accumulations in the esophagus, perform a detailed inspection of the esophagus by retracting the endoscope from the gastroesophageal junction. During this process, suction should be used, and gentle flushing performed to prevent mucus, saliva, or other debris from interfering with the assessment of the esophageal aspect. The esophagus should be assessed in a fully insufflated state to accurately describe and capture the EREFS signs. Full insufflation of the esophagus is essential to accurately describe and reflect the endoscopic signs of active EoE, such as edema, depth of furrows, and the severity of ring formation in the EREFS scoring system [ 30 ]. Another challenge can be the detection of strictures or esophageal narrowing in EoE patients. It is certainly not a problem to detect strictures when the endoscope cannot pass through; the challenge lies in identifying nonobstructive strictures and determining the diameter of the esophagus. Stenosis and/or strictures can occur in all segments of the esophagus. Furthermore, they can be focal or multifocal, or there can be diffuse narrowing of the esophagus in EoE [ 31 ]. In such situations, tactile sensation during endoscopy can be helpful. Does it feel like there is resistance or is the endoscope advancing more slowly? These can be clues indicating the presence of strictures or stenosis or esophageal narrowing [ 30 ].

Conclusion This article highlights the significance of the patient’s history of dysphagia in EoE, the use of the EREFS scoring system for endoscopic evaluation, and the importance of thorough and optimal esophageal examination during endoscopy. EoE patients often experience dysphagia for solid foods and other sometimes unspecific symptoms for years, which can lead to delayed diagnosis, primarily due to the avoidance strategies they adopt. The endoscopic examination reveals various structural changes in the esophagus, and the EREFS scoring system helps quantify these findings, aiding in diagnosis and monitoring of treatment. Even in cases of atypical symptoms or when the esophagus appears normal during endoscopy, step biopsies are strongly recommended. Proper endoscopic technique, including full insufflation of the esophagus, is crucial for accurate endoscopic assessment using the EREFS. Detecting strictures or narrowing can be challenging but important. Biopsy collection is essential, with guidelines recommending multiple biopsies from various esophageal locations. In summary, a comprehensive and thorough patient history, the EREFS scoring system, careful endoscopic examination, and adequate biopsy collection are essential for diagnosing and managing EoE in adults.

ABSTRACT Background Endoscopy with histopathological assessment of esophageal biopsies is the cornerstone for the diagnosis and phenotypic characterization of eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE).

Objective To evaluate temporal trends in endoscopic assessment and biopsy sampling practices for EoE in a large European cohort and their association with temporal trends in diagnostic delay (DD). Methods A cross‐sectional analysis was conducted using multicenter data from the EoE CONNECT registry. Endoscopic findings and biopsy data at diagnosis were analyzed. Temporal trends in biopsy strategies, EREFS implementation, and DD were assessed. Diagnostic sensitivity of individual esophageal segments and their combinations was evaluated in patients undergoing multi‐segment sampling. Associations between guideline publication and biopsy practices were analyzed using logistic regression models.

Results A total of 3298 patients were included. Biopsies were obtained from one esophageal segment in 12.6% of patients, two segments in 63.6%, and three segments in 23.8%. Adherence to guideline‐recommended biopsy strategies improved over time, with reduced single‐segment sampling and increased use of ≥ 2 segments. Distal esophageal biopsies provided the highest diagnostic sensitivity, and sampling that included the distal segment achieved sensitivity above 97%, particularly when combined with middle esophageal biopsies. EREFS reporting increased from 88–90% to over 98% in recent years. DD decreased significantly over time (approximately 0.7 years per calendar year), accompanied by a shift from mixed/stricturing to inflammatory phenotypes.

Conclusion Increased alignment with international guidelines, reflected by standardized endoscopic reporting and multi‐segment biopsy protocols, was associated with improved diagnostic sensitivity, reduced DD, and fewer fibrostricturing presentations. Key Summary

Summarise the established knowledge on this subject ◦ Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic disease characterized by esophagus dysfunction and eosinophil‐predominant inflammation of the esophageal mucosa, which is patchily distributed along the organ. ◦ Patients with EoE experience prolonged diagnostic delays across all reported countries, and published trends of small studies suggest that adherence to clinical guidelines may reduce the time to diagnosis. ◦ Data on the extent to which real‐world EoE diagnostic practices adhere to clinical practice guideline recommendations, and on their impact on patient outcomes over time, remain limited.

What are the significant and/or new findings of this study? ◦ Compliance with guideline‐recommended biopsy strategies increased over time, with reduced reliance on single‐segment endoscopic sampling and greater use of biopsies from ≥ 2 esophageal segments following the 2017 guideline publication. ◦ Distal esophageal biopsies yielded the highest diagnostic sensitivity; sampling protocols that included the distal segment achieved sensitivity exceeding 97%, particularly when combined with mid‐esophageal biopsies. ◦ Standardized reporting of endoscopic findings using the EREFS classification increased from 88% to over 98% in recent years. ◦ Diagnostic delay in EoE decreased significantly over time (by approximately 0.7 years per calendar year), resulting in fewer patients presenting with mixed or fibrostricturing phenotypes at diagnosis, and a corresponding increase in inflammatory presentations.

1 Introduction Eosinophilic esophagitis (EoE) is a chronic, immune‐mediated disease defined by symptoms of esophageal dysfunction and dense eosinophil infiltration in the esophageal mucosa. [ 1 ] Its global epidemiology has expanded rapidly, [ 2 ] and it has transitioned from a rare disease to a common disorder, with a ninefold increase in prevalence. [ 3 ] In fact, EoE represents the most common cause of dysphagia among children and young adults, and is the second cause of chronic dysphagia after gastroesophageal reflux disease (GERD). [ 2 ] Since EoE was first described in the early 1990s, [ 4 , 5 ] diagnostic approaches have evolved considerably. Early definitions emphasized mucosal eosinophil infiltration ranging between 5–30 eosinophils per high‐power field (eos/HPF), [ 6 ] until the first consensus guidelines in 2007 [ 7 ] formally established the ≥ 15 eos/hpf threshold. Recognition of the patchy distribution of eosinophilic infiltration along the esophagus [ 8 ] supported the adoption of multi‐site biopsies. [ 9 ]

Historically, proton pump inhibitors (PPIs) were used diagnostically to exclude GERD, [ 10 ] but since the 2017 international guidelines [ 1 ] they have been redefined as a first‐line therapeutic option [ 11 ]. Because EoE presents with heterogeneous symptoms that limit clinical diagnostic accuracy, [ 12 , 13 ] recent guidelines have emphasized a multimodal diagnostic strategy integrating clinical, histologic and endoscopic criteria, as endoscopic features were recognized as biologically relevant. [ 14 ] Accordingly, current recommendations [ 1 , 14 , 15 ] advocate the use of standardized endoscopic reporting systems such as EREFS, [ 16 ] and define EoE by the combination of dysphagia symptoms with histologic evidence of ≥ 15 eos/hpf in esophageal mucosa, obtained from at least six biopsies across a minimum of two segments along the esophagus.

Over almost two decades, multiple international guidelines, [ 1 , 14 , 15 , 17 ] national guidelines, [ 18 , 19 , 20 ] consensus statements, [ 7 , 21 , 22 , 23 , 24 , 25 ] and technical reviews [ 26 , 27 ] have structured the basis for EoE diagnosis and management. Although diagnosis of EoE has improved over time in Europe, [ 28 , 29 ] other works highlight irregular adherence to these recommendations, [ 30 , 31 , 32 ] resulting in underdiagnosis with a parallel influence on diagnostic delay (DD). [ 33 , 34 ] Observational studies describing real‐world diagnostic practices in EoE are scarce. Therefore, in this study, we sought to describe temporal trends in endoscopic assessment and biopsy practices in a large cohort of European EoE patients and to evaluate changes in DD throughout the study period.

2 Material and Methods 2.1 Study Design and Dataset Here we performed a cross‐sectional analysis of multicenter, prospectively‐collected data at EoE CONNECT, the European registry for EoE supported by EUREOS (European Consortium for Eosinophilic Diseases of the GI Tract). EoE CONNECT constitutes a large, clinically reliable source of EoE management‐related clinical data with public registering protocols and definitions. [ 35 ] On October 6th, 2025, 4663 patient IDs were retrieved from the EoE CONNECT registry. After applying predefined eligibility criteria (Figure 1 , Supporting Information S1 ), 3298 patients were included.

FIGURE 1 Patient selection flowchart for the EoE CONNECT registry analysis. To evaluate changes in clinical practice and adherence to diagnostic standards, the 2017 guidelines [ 1 ] were used as the reference, as they represent the first multi‐society, evidence‐based document developed using the GRADE methodology. This article was drafted according to STROBE guidelines for observational studies to ensure the quality of reporting [ 36 ].

2.2 Variables and Definitions The following variables were analyzed: age at diagnosis, sex, country and hospital of diagnosis, year of: symptom onset, diagnosis, endoscopy and histology reports; symptoms at diagnosis, Dysphagia Symptom Score (DSS), overall EREFS score and components (Edema, Rings, Exudates, Furrows and Stenosis), esophageal segment biopsied for diagnosis (proximal, middle and distal esophagus) and histology results. Definitions of hospital caseload, diagnostic delay, peak eosinophil count, pathologic biopsy and EoE phenotype are detailed in Supporting Information S1 .

2.3 Statistical Analysis Continuous and categorical variables were compared with non‐parametric and chi‐square tests as appropriate. Temporal trends were analyzed using linear regression, and the association between guideline‐defined periods and multi‐segment biopsy sampling using logistic regression models. Detailed statistical methods are provided in Supporting Information S1 . Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05; analyses were performed in SPSS v25.0 and GraphPad Prism v9.5.1.

2.4 Ethical Considerations The study adhered to the principles outlined in the Helsinki Declaration, which sets ethical guidelines for human‐related research. EoE CONNECT obtained approval from the Ethics Research Committee of Hospital Universitario de La Princesa (Madrid, Spain) as Central committee and from the corresponding committee in each participating center. Written informed consent from all patients or their legal guardians was obtained.

3 Results 3.1 Study Cohort and Baseline Characteristics A total of 3298 patients with confirmed EoE were included after application of predefined eligibility criteria (Figure 1 ). These patients were enrolled from 50 hospitals across four European countries participating in the EoE CONNECT registry, with data recorded up to October 6th 2025. 3.2 Biopsy Sampling Practices and Diagnostic Sensitivity Across Esophageal Segments At diagnosis, biopsies were obtained from a single esophageal segment in 417 patients (12.6%), from two segments in 2096 (63.6%), and from all three in 785 (23.8%), with a mean of 2.11 (SD 0.59) sampled segments per patient.

To assess the influence of guideline publication on sampling practices, patients were stratified into six diagnostic periods defined by major guidelines publication years (2007, [ 7 ] 2011, [ 22 ] 2013 [ 17 ], 2017 [ 1 ] and 2022 [ 18 , 37 ]). The proportion of patients undergoing biopsies from ≥ 2 esophageal segments significantly differed between time periods ( p < 0.001), increasing to more than 90.4% after 2018 (Figure 2A ). The odds of multi‐segment biopsy increased across periods compared with the ≤ 2007 reference group, with statistically significant associations observed in the 2018–2022 and 2023–2025 sub‐periods, reflecting a continuous and cumulative adoption of the 2017 guideline recommendations (Table 2 ). A linear regression analysis confirmed a significant increase in the proportion of patients undergoing ≥ 2 segment sampling over time (B = 1.22% per year; p < 0.001)(Supporting Information S1 : Figure S1). Sensitivity analyses repeating the same logistic regression with the 2008–2011, 2012–2013, and 2014–2017 periods as alternative reference categories yielded fully consistent results, (Supporting Information S1 . Multi‐segment sampling was significantly more frequent in high‐ than in low‐volume centers (Figure 2B ), and the proportion of ≥ 2‐segment biopsies increased significantly after 2017 in both groups (Table 3 ), reflecting broad adherence to updated guidelines.

Across all centres, distal biopsies were the most frequently sampled site and yielded the highest proportion of pathologic findings, confirming a distal‐to‐proximal gradient of disease activity (Figure 2C ). This was validated in the subgroup of patients with three‐segment sampling (n = 785) (Figure S2). Since multi‐segment biopsy is convenient, we evaluated the frequencies of segment combinations. Proximal + distal sampling was the most common combination (86.7%), followed by distal + middle (11.4%) and proximal + middle (1.9%). In patients undergoing three‐segment sampling ( n = 785), 66.7% showed above‐threshold eosinophilia (≥ 15 eos/hpf) at all sites. Among those with isolated eosinophilia in one out of the three segments (14.4%), the distal site was most informative (64.6% of pathologic biopsies), and the proximal least (14.2% of pathologic biopsies) (Figure 2D ). When patients were dichotomized into pediatric and adult groups, pediatric patients showed a higher frequency of proximal esophageal involvement compared with adults (81.1% vs. 72.4%; p = 0.02). No differences in segment‐specific pathologic findings were observed according to sex.

Then, we evaluated the diagnostic sensitivity of different 2‐segment combinations in the three‐segment sampling group ( n = 785). Distal + middle sampling achieved the highest sensitivity for EoE diagnosis (97.9%, 95% CI 96.97–98.96%), followed by distal + proximal (97.0%, 95% CI 95.74–98.15%) and middle + proximal segments (90.7%, 95% CI 88.67–92.73%). Differences in diagnostic sensitivity between 2‐segment combinations were explored by pairwise analysis across strategies. When middle + proximal was compared with either distal + middle or distal + proximal combinations, differences were statistically significant ( p < 0.001), but no when both combinations included the distal segment (distal + middle vs. distal + proximal; p = 0.27).

3.3 Temporal Trends in EREFS Implementation and Endoscopic Phenotypes The analysis of EREFS score implementation included data from 2014 onward, as the EREFS classification was published in 2013. [ 16 ] Over the study period, data showed a clear and progressive improvement in EREFS score reported across participating centers. In the earliest years of the registry, ∼10% of patients lacked a documented EREFS score, but this percentage steadily decreased to less than 1% by 2025 (Figure 3 ). This downward trend persisted following the publication of the 2017 European EoE guidelines, regardless of the hospital category (Table 3 ).

3.4 Diagnostic Delay Trends Over Time The analysis of DD included all patients with available data on the year of symptom onset ( n = 2810). Linear regression analysis revealed a statistically significant inverse association between the year of symptom onset and DD ( p < 0.001), with DD decreasing by approximately 8.5 months per calendar year (Figure 4A ). This temporal trend paralleled a progressive decline in mixed/stricturing phenotypes and a corresponding increase in inflammatory presentations (Figure 4B ). A consistent temporal trend was observed in both low‐ and high‐volume hospitals after 2017 (Table 3 ). The increase in inflammatory phenotype was statistically significant in both settings, whereas a significant reduction in the mixed/stricturing phenotype was observed only in high‐volume hospitals ( p = 0.002). These findings suggest a more pronounced association of reduced DD on phenotype distribution in high‐volume centers.

4 Discussion This study provides the most comprehensive evaluation of temporal changes in endoscopic assessment and biopsy sampling at EoE diagnosis, showing improved guideline adherence and diagnostic performance of biopsy strategies. These advances were paralleled by reduced DD, particularly in mixed/stricturing phenotypes, reflecting the growing integration of evidence‐based practices across Europe. The 2017 European guidelines were used as the reference, as they were the first multi‐society, evidence‐graded document defining standardized diagnostic criteria. [ 1 ] Subsequent publications reinforced multi‐segment sampling and standardized EREFS reporting without changing the core 2017 diagnostic recommendations. [ 18 , 37 ] Accordingly, improved biopsy practices after 2017 reflect cumulative guideline adoption. The updated 2025 American guidelines [ 14 ] were not considered, as their recent publication precluded meaningful influence during the study period. The only national EoE guidelines available among participating countries, published in Italy [ 24 ] and France [ 25 ], reiterate the same diagnostic recommendations established in 2017 without introducing a novel approach.

The progressive increase in the number of esophageal segments sampled over time, especially after major international guidelines, reflects growing awareness of the need for tissue sampling to improve diagnostic reliability. This evolution aligns with the inherently patchy distribution of eosinophilic inflammation in EoE [ 8 , 38 ] where inflamed areas often lie adjacent to histologically normal mucosa, so single‐site sampling may yield false negatives and underestimate disease burden. Recent studies in adult [ 39 , 40 ] and pediatric cohorts [ 41 ] confirmed this heterogeneity showing discordant histologic results along the esophagus, agreeing in a denser eosinophilia and more common pathologic findings in the distal segment compared to middle and proximal locations. Therefore, multi‐segment biopsy protocols are pivotal to achieve accurate histologic diagnosis of EoE. Since the first consensus document [ 38 ], and subsequent guidelines [ 1 , 14 , 21 , 22 ] sampling of distal and proximal esophagus were recommended to maximize diagnosis. However, evidence supporting optimal location for biopsy sampling remains limited, particularly from studies evaluating patients with three‐segment sampling at diagnosis, thereby minimizing bias due to missing segment data. Our study comprising 785 of such patients, considerably expands previous works that addressed this question with over 60 patients [ 39 , 41 ] and a third, more recent, with a larger cohort (263 patients) but largely composed of patients in clinical remission or post‐treatment, limiting direct comparability with diagnostic‐stage disease [ 42 ]. Nonetheless, previous and current data agree on a distal‐to‐proximal sensitivity gradient. Distal samples most frequently showed histologic activity, with progressively lower positivity rates in middle and proximal segments. In our cohort, sensitivity reached 91.8% in the distal, 85.5% in the middle, and 74.9% in the proximal esophagus. For biopsy combinations, inclusion of the distal segment yielded sensitivity above 97%, whereas the proximal + middle combination was considerably lower (90.7%). Nevertheless, three‐segment sampling still provided an incremental diagnostic benefit of about 2%, according to the prevalence of isolated proximal eosinophilic involvement. These findings support proximal biopsies and comprehensive three‐segment sampling, particularly in pediatric patients, in whom proximal involvement was significantly more frequent. A prospective pediatric cohort similarly showed that combining distal biopsies with either middle or proximal sampling achieves ∼98% diagnostic yield, whereas mid‐proximal combinations remain suboptimal [ 41 ]. Taken together, these findings indicate that distal sampling is recommended for optimal diagnostic yield, and the choice between middle or proximal as the second segment is diagnostically equivalent and may be guided by the presence of endoscopic features or practical considerations. However, proximal sampling captures the small proportion of patients with isolated proximal disease and is particularly relevant in pediatric patients, in whom proximal involvement was more frequent than in adults in our cohort (81.1% vs 72.4%; p = 0.02). Therefore, three‐segment sampling remains the preferred standard whenever clinically feasible. This may be especially important in children and adolescents, in whom the greater frequency of proximal involvement could increase the risk of missed diagnoses when proximal biopsies are omitted.

EREFS implementation across EoE CONNECT centers reflected improved standardization of endoscopic assessment. Since its introduction in 2013 [ 43 ], EREFS scoring increased from about 88–90% to more than 98% by 2025, while missing reports declined. This likely reflects awareness of structured reporting, reinforced by the 2017 European guidelines and subsequent consensus recommendations [ 21 ]. Both high‐ and low‐volume centers showed parallel improvements in biopsy sampling and EREFS documentation, suggesting widespread adoption of standardized protocols and a general enhancement in diagnostic quality across Europe. Likewise, diagnostic delay and trend in phenotype distribution were not influenced by hospital‐volume, indicating that temporal trends were not exclusively driven by highly experienced centers. The temporal analysis revealed a progressive reduction in DD and a marked shift in endoscopic phenotypes, with a decline in mixed/stricturing forms and an increase in inflammatory presentations. Chronic, untreated inflammation is known to drive fibrotic remodeling and luminal narrowing, a process clearly documented in previous studies showing the prevalence of strictures rose from 19% among patients diagnosed within two years of symptom onset to 52% in those with delays exceeding 20 years [ 16 ]. Similarly, a multi‐center Dutch cohort reported a 9% increase in the odds of stricture formation for each additional year of delay, with fibrostricturing forms rising from 19% to 92% across the same interval [ 44 ]. Our results were consistent with this continuum, as shorter DDs were accompanied by fewer fibrostricturing presentations, particularly among mixed/stricturing phenotypes, suggesting that earlier recognition may prevent progression to advanced structural remodeling. This association was further exemplified by patients diagnosed after food impaction, who showed a threefold longer delay than those without impaction (12 vs. 4 years, p = 0.009) and significantly higher total, inflammatory, and fibrostricturing EREFS scores [ 45 ]. The progressive decline in DD mirrored the improvement previously described in the EoE CONNECT network, where median delay decreased from 12.7 years before 2007 to 0.7 years after 2017, alongside a reduction in fibrostricturing phenotypes (from 41% to 16%) and lower EREFS sub‐scores [ 29 ]. This interpretation must, however, be tempered by the parallel improvement in EREFS documentation observed over the study period. The proportion of patients with sufficient EREFS data for phenotype classification rose progressively across the diagnostic periods (Table 2 ), from 65.8% in ≤ 2007 to 96.7% in 2023–2025, meaning that phenotype distributions in earlier periods are based on a smaller and potentially non‐representative subset. Part of the apparent shift toward inflammatory phenotypes may therefore reflect more complete and consistent documentation of subtle endoscopic features in recent years, in addition to a reduction in advanced fibrostricturing presentations only partly driven by earlier diagnosis. Collectively, these data indicate that the dissemination of clinical guidelines and increased physician awareness have translated into measurable advances in the timeliness and accuracy of EoE diagnosis across Europe.

This study had several notable strengths. It relied on the EoE CONNECT registry, a structured and high‐quality source of real‐world clinical data, representing the largest multicenter evaluation of endoscopic and biopsy practices at EoE diagnosis in Europe. The broad temporal coverage (1991–2025) enabled the assessment of genuine longitudinal trends in diagnostic behavior, while the large sample size provided robust power to evaluate segment‐specific diagnostic performance. Several limitations should be acknowledged. Participating centers likely had a greater‐than‐average interest and expertise in EoE, introducing a potential expertise bias that may limit generalizability to less specialized settings. Moreover, as the majority of centers are from Spain (83%), the trends primarily reflect Spanish, and to a lesser extent, Italian clinical practice. The classification of centers by volume (cut‐off 200 patients) is necessarily arbitrary, and all participating centers likely share a higher‐than‐average interest in EoE management, reinforcing the potential expertise bias of the analysis. The registry did not capture the exact number of biopsy fragments obtained per site, a determinant of diagnostic sensitivity [ 46 ], nor did it distinguish between the patient‐ and physician‐dependent components of DD, which have recently been recognized as distinct phases in the diagnostic pathway [ 47 ]. Histological assessment relied on peak eosinophil counts rather than systematic EoEHSS grading, limiting the evaluation of epithelial injury and remodeling beyond eosinophil density. However, this was unlikely to affect phenotype classification, which was mainly based on clinical‐endoscopic rather than histological fibrosis assessment. In addition, factors influencing biopsy sampling strategies at the individual patient level could not be assessed as this information is not systematically collected in the EoE CONNECT registry. Information on symptom onset relied solely on patient self‐report and may therefore be subject to recall bias, especially among patients with earlier symptom onset before 2010. However, these patients represented only 17.1% of the total cohort, so the potential impact of this bias may be limited. Furthermore, our study described temporal associations but cannot establish direct causal relationships between guideline publication and patient outcomes such as DD. The effect in DD and changes on phenotype distribution over time is likely a reflection of the cumulative integration of evidence‐based diagnostic practices and clinical guidelines adherence into the evolving clinical environment.

Here we offered the most comprehensive real‐world overview of how diagnostic practices for EoE have evolved across Europe. Over more than three decades, clinical practice progressively aligned with international guidelines, measured here as the adoption of standardized endoscopic reporting and multi‐segment biopsy protocols. We reported, with the largest study cohort to date, that distal containing sampling exhibits the greatest sensitivity, especially when combined with middle segments, supporting optimized biopsy strategies. Finally, the concurrent decline in DD and fibrostricturing forms indicates that earlier recognition is becoming a measurable outcome of improved clinical awareness and guideline‐based management.

Background Food impactions in the esophagus are gastroenterologic emergencies. Their incidence is suspected to increase. Standard therapy is endoscopic removal. According to European guidelines from 2016, gently pushing the food forward with the endoscope is safe and efficient. This has recently been doubted, and a retrograde extraction of the food bolus was supposed to be safer.
Methods We retrospectively analyzed all food impactions in our database over 16 years regarding incidence per year, age, sex, underlying disease, method of removal, success rate, and safety.

Results From 2008 to 2024, 99 patients were included. Incidence of food impactions increased logarithmically from one per year to 22 per year (p < 0.001). Seventy-nine patients were male (80%; p < 0.001). Underlying diseases were reflux-associated lesions, eosinophilic esophagitis, pseudo­diverticulosis, hernia, achalasia, candidiasis, and others. Fifty-five were pushed forward prior to 2016, afterwards it were 74 (56% and 75% respectively; p < 0.001). Success rate was 100 percent for all techniques. We observed two minor adverse events in the forward-pushing group vs. one in the extraction group (not significant).

Conclusion Our data confirms that food obstructions are on the rise and that the vast majority of patients are male. There is no typical underlying disease but a wide variety of rare diseases which together form the basis for the increase. Pushing forward is as safe as is extracting the food, so we see no necessity to change the existing guidelines.

Zusammenfassung Hintergrund Bolus-Impaktationen sind gastroenterologische Notfälle mit vermutlich steigender Inzidenz. Standardtherapie ist die endoskopische Entfernung. Hierbei ist gemäß Leitlinie des Jahres 2016 das sanfte Vorschieben des Bolus sicher und effizient. Dies wurde kürzlich angezweifelt und die retrograde Extraktion als sicherer empfohlen. Methoden Wir analysierten retrospektiv alle Bolusereignisse in unserer Datenbank über 16 Jahre hinsichtlich Inzidenz, Alter, Geschlecht, Grunderkrankung, Entfernungsmethode, Erfolgsrate und Sicherheit.

Ergebnisse 99 Bolusereignisse wurden ausgewertet. Von 2008 bis 2024 stieg die jährliche Inzidenz logarithmisch von 1 auf 22 (p<0,001). 79 Patienten waren männlich (80%; p<0,001). Grunderkrankungen waren Reflux, eosinophile Ösophagitis, Pseudodivertikulose, Hernie, Achalasie, Candidiasis und andere. Vor 2016 wurden 55 Boli vorgeschoben (56%), danach 74 (75%). Die Erfolgsrate lag für beide Techniken bei 100 Prozent. Wir beobachteten zwei kleinere Komplikationen in der Vorschub-Gruppe und eine in der Extraktions-Gruppe (nicht signifikant).

Diskussion Unsere Daten bestätigen die Vermutung, dass Bolusereignisse deutlich zugenommen haben, und dass die überwiegende Mehrheit der Patienten männlich ist. Grundlage ist weniger eine einzelne typische Erkrankung, sondern eine Vielzahl eher seltener Erkrankungen zusammengenommen. Bezüglich Erfolg und Sicherheit sind Vorschub und Extraktion gleichwertig. Wir sehen daher keine Notwendigkeit, die bestehenden Leitlinien zu ändern.
